items.description_html:
Cohance Life Sciences , DMF filing activity picking up now , just to see what they are filing

1) Exatecan mesylate (also known as DX-8951f) is a man-made, water-soluble drug derived from camptothecin. It works as a cancer-fighting agent by blocking topoisomerase I, an enzyme cells need to copy their DNA. It is also used to build payloads for antibody-drug conjugates

2) Irinotecan hydrochloride trihydrate is a prescription anti-cancer chemotherapy medication classified as a topoisomerase I inhibitor. It works by blocking an enzyme called topoisomerase I, which stops cancer cells from copying their DNA and causes them to die, Used to treat cancer of the colon or rectum

3) Pyridostigmine bromide USP is a cholinesterase inhibitor that treats muscle weakness in myasthenia gravis. It stops an enzyme from breaking down acetylcholine, which helps nerve impulses pass better to muscles

4) Propafenone Hydrochloride USP is a Class 1C antiarrhythmic medication manufactured to United States Pharmacopeia quality standards. It stabilizes heart rhythms by blocking sodium channels in myocardial cells. It is prescribed to treat serious heart rhythm disorders like atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmias

Extacen is the one that looks very interesting because of the ADC depth and very little filings from other players

Just reading what they are up to on filings we will be tracking this closely on incremental filings

items.title: Spinny’s original thesis was that India’s used-car market was broken for both buyers and sellers. Its first answer was a consumer-to-consumer (C2C) ...
items.description_html:
Spinny’s original thesis was that India’s used-car market was broken for both buyers and sellers.

Its first answer was a consumer-to-consumer (C2C) managed marketplace.

Spinny would inspect and curate cars, help sellers find buyers, enable price discovery and manage the transaction end to end.

But the team soon realised they were solving the wrong side of the market.

At the time, used cars were in short supply and buyers were plentiful.

Sellers could list a car on platforms like OLX and receive hundreds of calls within 30 minutes.

Buyers had the much harder problem like inconsistent quality, lack of transparency and also the stigma attached with buying a used car.

“The bottom line was that solving for this category is all about solving for buyers. It has to be a demand-first, full-stack model where you own the entire value chain end to end,” Spinny founder Niraj Singh says.

That realisation would become the basis for Spinny’s pivot.

More in Legendary Pivots, our series in collaboration with SeedToScale by Accel.


SeedToScale: "It's not about preserving a little bit of early success."

@myspinny was scaling as a consumer-to-consumer managed marketplace. Nothing in the numbers said stop.

PHOTO OF THE DAY:

📌It is raining this monsoon in Delhi. Not just water, but also potholes, like in monsoons past.

📌As the capital saw heavy spells of rain in July and August, the asphalt wore off on several important routes, once again pointing to poor quality materials used in construction.

📌According to data tabled by the Union Ministry of Road Transport and Highways in the Lok Sabha in February this year, deaths due to potholes increased by over 53 per cent since 2020.

📌A total of 1,555 persons died in 2020 in pothole-related road accidents, which increased to 2,385 fatalities in 2024. This translates into over six road deaths due to potholes daily.

📌Yet come every monsoon, and the same old story repeats.

items.title: Manyavar: 3 reasons they close their stores – "I think regarding closures, I have never faced a reason for a closure to be competition. So, there are...
items.description_html:
Manyavar: 3 reasons they close their stores –

"I think regarding closures, I have never faced a reason for a closure to be competition.

So, there are primarily 3 types of closures that we have in the company.

The number 1 of closures right now is that the market has shifted. We've already opened a store in the newer side of the market. And while 3 years ago, this store was still doing decent numbers, over a course of time, we are now in a situation where we either renovate the store or close it. And closing it makes more sense because we don't see growth in that market overall in the coming few years.

The second reason is that we have opened a larger store in a bigger town in the neighborhood. So, what I mean by that is, if there is a cluster of 4 Tier 3 cities. And we open a very large store in 1 Tier 3 city, then people wish to travel to that Tier 3 city rather than buying from their store. This is the second reason.

And the final reason, which is the smallest of all, is that the store never did well from day 1 of us opening it, because it was a pure mistake from a new store-opening perspective. So, these are the 3 reasons that primarily play a role in store closures."

Src - Q1Fy27 Concall, No reco

items.description_html:
The @IEA has once again revised historical annual data for oil consumption (it does so every August), resulting in some significant upgrades to global demand.

The net result is that 20025 oil consumption is now estimated at 104.8m b/d (that's ~300,000 b/d higher than the last estimate, and ***a huge 1.1m b/d higher*** than where the IEA pegged a year ago 2025 demand).

Despite the huge revision to demand forecasts, the IEA still sees the market last year as oversupplied, with supply running at 106.3m b/d on average.

The changes also mean that the 105.7m b/d of oil consumption that the IEA now anticipates for 2027 is **higher** than the absolute peak oil demand it forecast a year ago (when it said that global oil consumption would peak in 2029 at 105.6m b/d).

RT Aditi Shrivastava
🚨 Accel, the first institutional investor in Flipkart, Swiggy and Freshworks, has closed its ninth India-specific fund at $550 million, just 18 months after raising $650 million.

Globally, Accel has gathered $3.5 billion across four new vehicles. The set includes a $1.35-billion growth pot that can invest across markets including India.

Deployment areas: Artificial intelligence will be the biggest new area of interest, while also continue betting on consumer, fintech and manufacturing.

A key development in Accel’s Indian portfolio is the growing number of IPOs-- Swiggy, Urban Company, Amagi, BlueStone and BlackBuck have all completed stock listings over the past two years.

Accel has sold shares worth an estimated Rs 2,000-2,500 crore ($210-262 million) across these five companies, according to The Arc’s calculations. Its remaining holdings in them are worth Rs 7,000-7,500 crore ($733-786 million).

More Accel bets are moving towards the public markets: Zetwerk and InfraMarket, Moneyview and RentoMojo.

The Arc spoke with Accel partners Shekhar Kirani, Anand Daniel and Rachit Parekh about the strategy behind the new $550-million India fund and where the firm sees opportunities emerging from AI.

items.title: TD Power - Q1FY27 First Cut Analysis: Blockbuster start to FY27* - TDPS posted its highest-ever quarterly revenue and order inflow. Consol. revenue gr...
items.description_html:
TD Power - Q1FY27 First Cut Analysis: Blockbuster start to FY27*

- TDPS posted its highest-ever quarterly revenue and order inflow. Consol. revenue grew +71% y/y to Rs6.40bn (v/s our estimate of Rs4.78bn), EBITDA +72% to Rs1.21bn (19.0% margin) and PAT +72% to Rs863mn (v/s our estimate of R650mn). Order inflow jumped +87% y/y to Rs7.34bn (93% exports), taking the order book to Rs22.07bn. BS stays net-cash (~Rs2.16bn) with negligible debt.

- TDPS has done second highest quarterly installations of 320 generators (after 354 reported in Q4FY25).

- Management upgraded FY27 revenue guidance to Rs26bn (Q1 achieved 24.6% of the revised FY27 guidance). The clear swing factor now is execution, not demand.

- Q1FY27 inflow of Rs7.34bn vs Rs3.91bn (+87% y/y), the highest-ever quarterly intake; run-rate has crossed Rs7bn/quarter. 93% of OI’s were from exports (Rs6.83bn), domestic inflows declined to Rs505mn from Rs1.34bn a year ago. Management attributes weak domestic to timing (esp. hydro) and expects recovery in coming quarters. Export order wins were from gas engine / gas turbine orders led by US data-center demand (repeat, high-volume, standardized programs from global OEMs); steam CPP orders incl. a 60 MW 2-pole generator; Hydro landed its largest-ever domestic order (4×16 MW vertical hydro for Africa project). US 60 Hz / data-center theme is now the structural growth engine and underpins the export tilt.

- Order book as of Q1FY27-end was at Rs22.07bn, with exports accounting for 73% of the total OB (giving visibility for next 4 quarters).

- Key questions to ask management: Commentary on the upcoming capex, execution outlook and the proposed fund raising plans.

- Continue to maintain our BUY rating on the stock. Would come out with revised numbers and a detailed note post the call scheduled today at 11.30am.

Brokerage note

items.description_html:
Another morning, another defence tech news story

A Mumbai start-up, Techno Defence, has developed a tiny 10-gram JT Cooler that cools missile IR seekers to nearly -196°C

This is highly strategic technology, reportedly controlled under the Missile Technology Control Regime and possessed by only a handful of countries such as the US, France, and Israel.

The journey started with a chance interaction with DRDO around 2017-18.

Funding under DRDO's Technology Development Fund came in 2020.

By 2023-24, the company had developed the product and handed it over to DRDO for successful trials.

And what I found even more interesting — this wasn't built with a massive factory or thousands of engineers.

A small team, specialised production techniques, cottage/small-scale industries, and extremely high-precision manufacturing helped crack it.

This is the India manufacturing story I keep talking about.

Not just Make in India.

Design in India. Develop in India. Manufacture in India. And eventually, Export from India. 🇮🇳

The opportunity in defence deep-tech is only getting bigger!

items.title: BREAKING: President Trump's capital gains tax cut discussions include "indexing" capital gains for inflation BEFORE taxes are calculated. This would m...
items.description_html:
BREAKING: President Trump's capital gains tax cut discussions include "indexing" capital gains for inflation BEFORE taxes are calculated.

This would mean that taxes would be applied on gains adjusted for inflation.

For example, if you purchased a stock for $100,000 and sold it 5 years later for $200,000.

Under the current system, you would owe capital gains taxes on the full $100,000 gain.

But, if cumulative inflation over those 5 years was 20%, your inflation-adjusted cost basis would rise to $120,000.

This means you would only owe capital gains taxes on the $80,000 REAL gain, rather than the $100,000 nominal gain.

Trump has also suggested exemptions for sales of homes worth $2 million or less from capital gains taxes.

We expect more details soon.

This means an average of -35,067 jobs have been revised out of previously reported data each month over this period.

June and May jobs numbers alone were revised down by a total of -103,000, the largest 2-month downward revision since July 2025.

This comes as June jobs were revised down by -37,000, to +20,000, while May jobs were revised down by -66,000, to +63,000.

The May jobs figure was revised down for the 2nd time, following a -43,000 downward revision last month from the initially reported +172,000 jobs.

If these revisions continue, June jobs could be revised into negative territory next month, which, combined with July's already reported -23,000 job loss, would mark the 2nd consecutive monthly decline in jobs, the first such occurrence since the 2020 pandemic.

Job market revisions are alarming.

items.title: We are witnessing the largest CapEx spending spree in history. Hyperscalers have committed a record $2.6 trillion in future spending across data cente...
items.description_html:
We are witnessing the largest CapEx spending spree in history.

Hyperscalers have committed a record $2.6 trillion in future spending across data center leases and equipment purchases.

This includes leases for data centers and power infrastructure that have not yet commenced, and existing purchase contracts for equipment and services.

These obligations do not appear on company balance sheets and are disclosed only in limited accounting footnotes, despite their enormous size and duration.

Alphabet, $GOOGL, has the largest total, with $811 billion in purchase commitments and $85 billion in leases not yet commenced, bringing its combined obligations to ~$896 billion.

By contrast, Oracle, $ORCL, has committed $32 billion to purchases, but $260 billion to leases that have not yet commenced, the largest lease obligation among the group, bringing its total to ~$292 billion.

The AI buildout has become one of the largest long-term capital commitments in corporate history.

items.title: Yatharth Hospitals - Execution Continues to Impress Q1FY27 REV: 393 Cr (+51% YoY) EBITDA: 92 Cr (+39% YoY) PAT: 45 Cr (+8% YoY) New hospitals are incr...
items.description_html:
Yatharth Hospitals - Execution Continues to Impress

Q1FY27
REV: 393 Cr (+51% YoY)
EBITDA: 92 Cr (+39% YoY)
PAT: 45 Cr (+8% YoY)

New hospitals are increasingly becoming the growth engine. Their contribution to group REV increased to 27% in Q1FY27 from just 9% in Q1FY26, while the existing hospitals grew 22% YoY.

The current reported margin understates the underlying profitability of the network. Cons. EBITDA margin is ~23%, but excluding the ramp-up losses of Model Town & Faridabad Sector-20, Adj EBITDA margin stands at ~28%. As the new hospitals move towards breakeven & maturity, this gap should progressively narrow.

Faridabad Sector-20 has been a strong proof of Yatharth's acquisition & integration capabilities. The 400 bed hospital achieved EBITDA breakeven in just 9 months. Latest monthly REV has already reached ~12-13 Cr with ARPOB of ~40k.

Model Town, Delhi is also ramping up strongly. Latest monthly REV is ~8 Cr & ARPOB has already moved close to 50k. Management expects the hospital to achieve EBITDA breakeven in H2FY27.

Agra has performed particularly well, delivering >20% EBITDA margin in its first full quarter of integration. Latest monthly REV is already ~9-10 Cr with ARPOB above 30k.

Group ARPOB increased 7% YoY to ~35k

Yatharth has built a network of 2,800+ beds including the upcoming Gurugram hospital & has laid out a roadmap to reach ~5,000 beds over the next 3 years.

The upcoming 250 bed hospital in Gurgaon is expected to commence operations in Q1FY28, with management indicating ARPOB potential of ~50k+.

Yatharth's journey over the last few quarters has been exceptional. The company has expanded aggressively through acquisitions, but the real positive is the pace at which the newly acquired hospitals are scaling up & moving towards profitability. A solid wealth creator since listing !

items.title: US housing affordability is deteriorating: The average 30Y fixed mortgage rate rose +3 basis points last week, to 6.69%, the highest since July 2025. ...
items.description_html:
US housing affordability is deteriorating:

The average 30Y fixed mortgage rate rose +3 basis points last week, to 6.69%, the highest since July 2025.

This marks the 5th consecutive weekly increase, with rates up +71 basis points since the Iran War began in late-February.

This comes as the 10Y Treasury yield, which mortgage lenders use to price 30Y loans, has surged +70 basis points over the same period, driven by inflation concerns.

On a $500,000 mortgage, this increase translates to more than +$200 in additional monthly principal and interest payments compared to late February, when rates briefly fell below 6% for the first time since 2022.

The 30Y fixed mortgage rate could rise to 7% for the first time since January 2025 before year-end if current inflationary pressures persist.

The US housing affordability crisis is worsening.

Global record highs have arrived.

The number of countries in the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI) making new 52-week highs is up to 28, the highest since February.

This figure has more than quadrupled since April.

Over this period, the MSCI ACWI has surged +20% to a fresh all-time high.

The index has also remained above its 80-week moving average for 16 consecutive months, highlighting strong momentum across global equities.

Furthermore, none of the 70 countries in the index are making new 52-week lows.

By comparison, 47 countries were making new 52-week highs in January, the highest number on record, suggesting the current breadth still has significant room to expand.

Global equity momentum is showing remarkable strength.

items.description_html:
Big Tech's AI spending is rising to levels rarely seen in modern history:

Amazon, $AMZN, Alphabet, $GOOGL, Meta, $META, Microsoft, $MSFT, and Oracle, $ORCL, are estimated to increase CapEx by +1.0 percentage point of US GDP in 2026, to a record 2.4%.

That compares with 1.0% of GDP spent on CapEx by broadcasting and telecommunications companies in 1999.

By 2027, Big Tech CapEx is projected to more than double to 3.1% of GDP, from 1.4% in 2025.

By comparison, broadcasting and telecom CapEx peaked at 1.2% of GDP in 2000.

To put this into perspective, Big Tech CapEx stood at 0.8% of GDP in 2024, the same level telecom CapEx recorded in 1997.

The AI investment boom is materially exceeding the capital spending surge of the Dot-Com era.

items.title: RT Peterson Institute: If Trump's tariffs on other countries end up too high compared with those on China, some supply chains that moved out of China ...
items.description_html:
RT Peterson Institute
If Trump's tariffs on other countries end up too high compared with those on China, some supply chains that moved out of China in the past year might find it advantageous to move back.
💡Lessons from Trump's 2025 tariffs on imports of phones vs. clothing from India & China:
📱In 2025, Trump imposed tariffs on smartphones from China but not India (figure 1 below).
🍎Apple responded to those tariffs on China by quickly sourcing iPhones from India.
📵Those smartphone tariffs were not universal. On Liberation Day, smartphones were exempted from those tariffs.
🍎This exemption incentivized Apple to maintain its sourcing switch away from China. Even when Trump increased overall tariffs on India to 50% in August 2025, he continued to exempt smartphones assembled in India.
📱iPhones assembled in China faced a 20% tariff that iPhones assembled in India did not.
📊Total US imports of smartphones in 2025 did not fall dramatically (figure 2 below).
📈By May 2025, nearly 2/3 of US smartphone imports were arriving from India, up from only 6% as late as October of 2024.
📱Between April 2025-February 2026, nearly half of US smartphone imports were from India.
💡Meanwhile...
👕In 2025, Trump imposed high tariffs on clothing from both China & India.
👖Trump's tariffs on India (both Liberation Day & August) did not exempt clothing.
👚US imports of clothing did not suddenly switch to India (Figure 3 below).
🧦By October 2025, US tariffs on clothing from India were higher than on clothing from China (Figure 4 below).
👗By the end of 2025, the US tariff differential between China & countries like Vietnam & Bangladesh was basically unchanged from pre-Trump 2.0 levels (Figure 4 again).
🧤For clothing, there was little new tariff incentive in 2025 to move a supply chain out of China to alternative destinations (see Figure 3 panel b).
💡Since the IEEPA decision...
➡️US import sourcing for smartphones & clothing has stabilized, but not yet changed dramatically, in response to the major US tariff adjustments beginning in February 2026.
💡Why Trump's next tariff moves could change the dynamics
3⃣0⃣1⃣: A new set of tariffs on 16 countries from ongoing Section 301 investigations into "excess capacity" may increase the tariff differential on imports from China relative to other key foreign suppliers...
...which could incentivize companies to find sources outside of China.
‼️OR Trump's new tariffs could incentivize US imports of certain products to move back to China.
❓Why?
🤔Suppose those upcoming Section 301 tariffs do not result in a significantly wide tariff differential favoring alternative sources, such as India.
‼️If a US company's competitors all source from China & the US tariff on alternative source countries remains too high, the desire to stay in business may force a company to buy from China too.
⚖️Especially if those 301 tariffs are more legally durable than the IEEPA tariffs, the reduction in uncertainty could convince companies to increase their import sourcing from China.
💡For the supply chain implications resulting from Trump's next tariffs & his Board of Trade...
...look for the size of product-level US tariff differentials between China & other major potential source countries.

items.title: Why Increasing Value Per kit important in Auto Ancs? 1. For decades, ancillary revenue was hostage to vehicle volumes. Every auto slowdown hit supplie...
items.description_html:
Why Increasing Value Per kit important in Auto Ancs?

1. For decades, ancillary revenue was hostage to vehicle volumes. Every auto slowdown hit suppliers directly. Content per vehicle breaks that link. Revenue starts compounding independent of how many cars a country actually sells.

2. The EV transition was supposed to be the industry's biggest risk. Single component suppliers tied to fuel systems, exhausts, and ICE only parts face real extinction risk. Suppliers building powertrain agnostic systems across plastics, mechatronics, and structures face none.

3. The scoreboard has changed. It's no longer how many units you sold. It's how much wallet share you own inside every vehicle that rolls off the line. That's the real KPI now.

4. This decouples ancillary earnings from the entire EV debate. Whether a market hits 20% EV penetration or 60% by 2030 stops being the question that decides who wins.

This is why Kit value per vehicle is the key metric to track in Auto Ancs going forward.

Its not about how many clients you have but how much more can you sell to the existing client

Disc: no recommendation to buy or sell. Mental models for different sectors.

Korea Times: "The South Korean surplus totaled $49.73 billion in June, up from the previous record of $38.61 billion in May."

These are incredibly large surpluses. This is why I have long argued that the problem isn't China. It is a global trading system that allows, and even rewards, countries that choose to suppress domestic demand in order to make their manufacturing sectors more competitive than those of their trading partners.

It does this by allowing them with no penalty to run the trade surpluses that force their trade partners to absorb the costs of their domestic policies. This is precisely what Keynes argued against at Bretton Woods.

items.title: RT Nimesh Shah: CLSA on SBI O-P, TP Raised to Rs 1325 Delivered a healthy all-rounded quarter. Domestic NIM expanded 7bps QoQ and was in-line with man...
items.description_html:
RT Nimesh Shah
CLSA on SBI
O-P, TP Raised to Rs 1325
Delivered a healthy all-rounded quarter.
Domestic NIM expanded 7bps QoQ and was in-line with management’s earlier full-year guidance.
As a result, NII beat estimate by 2%
Moreover, higher fee income and lower Opex resulted in a 12% core PPOP beat.
Loan growth remained healthy at 18%-19% YoY & was broad-based across segments
Latter is an area where some private sector peers have lagged.
Similar to peers, asset quality improved with its gross/net slippage ratio down c.20bps YoY; its lowest 1Q level in several years
Raise FY27-29 PAT estimates 2%-6% on higher NII & lower provisions

Bernstein on SBI
Market Perform, TP Rs 1300
Reported a broadly steady quarter, supported by broad-based loan growth, healthy NII growth driven by a sequential improvement in NIMs, and stable asset quality.
Deposit growth remained relatively subdued (10% YoY), resulting in a higher LDR.
Despite a seasonal rise in slippages, higher recoveries and upgrades kept credit costs stable and supported a modest improvement in asset quality.
Strong fee income growth (21% YoY) and modest operating expense growth (5% YoY) helped RoA improve modestly to 1.11% during quarter

CITI On SBI
Buy, TP Rs 1300
Domestic NIMs rebounded 7bps QoQ to 3.00% (global: 2.86%), as easing CoDs and improving yields vindicated management's 3% NIM target.
Earnings beat expectations, rising 10% YoY / 7% QoQ, underpinned by 14% YoY (6% QoQ) NII growth, Rs43.2bn treasury gains, and contained opex (+5% YoY / -14% QoQ).
Slippages edged up seasonally to Rs70.5bn (0.6%), with Rs14.5–15.0bn pulled back.
Credit costs of 41bps marginally above estimates, reflecting deliberate front-loading of PLI provisions.
Advances re-accelerated to 19% YoY (~2.3% QoQ), driven by retail/SME/Agri, with corporate flat QoQ.
Management targets US$10bn FCNR(B) deposits with negligible NIM impact, reiterating 3% domestic NIM and 14–15% credit growth guidance for FY27.

HSBC on SBI
Buy, TP Rs 1310
1Q an all-round beat led by strong NIM, core fees, contained expenses and credit costs
Lift EPS by 9-14% for FY27-29e on stronger-than-estimated NIM momentum and better-than-estimated cost control
TP raised on stronger-thanestimated core performance and healthy growth outlook

MS on SBI
EW, TP Rs 1070
Raised forecasts as reversed some of sharp cut in NIM after the 4QF26 miss, given a better outcome in 1QF27.
Assume NIM to remain largely stable from here, though will watch this given volatility in recent quarters
Valuation is full relative to sustainable ROA, ROE.

JPM on SBI
OW, TP Rs 1290
Strong 1Q’FY27 with broad-based beats across key operating parameters.
NII at Rs 469.9bn (+14% y/y, +6% q/q) came +3% vs JPM, PPOP at Rs 335.3bn (+10% y/y, +21% q/q) came +13% vs JPM, PAT at Rs 211.2bn (+10% y/y, +7% q/q) came +15% vs JPM
SBI’s loan growth at 19% y/y came in +1% vs JPMe with SBI raising growth guidance to 14-15% y/y (vs 12-14% earlier), underscoring SBI's confidence in the strong growth momentum.
Credit costs at 41bps also came in lower vs JPMe of 42bps

Macquarie on SBI
O-P, TP Rs 1150
PAT rose 10% YoY to Rs211bn, beating estimates on resilient reported margins (2.86%), tight opex (with cost to income at 47% vs MQe 50%) and stable 27bps credit costs.
Non-interest income fell 8% YoY on weak trading and forex income, though commissions rose at a healthy pace.
Non-loan provisions jumped 5x YoY to Rs13bn as mgmt amortised performance incentive hit across qtrs as against the exit quarter earlier.
Loan growth was strong at 19% YoY (aided by benign base; 2% QoQ), matching the system and led by SME and agri
Corporate segment was flat QoQ due to T-bill-to-MCLR repricing.
Mgmt lifted FY27 guidance to 14–15% (from 13–15%).

Jefferies on SBI
Buy, TP Rs 1320
Q1 Profit at Rs211bn was ahead of est aided by higher NII, treasury and lower opex.
Rebound of domestic NIM aided NII growth of 15% YoY, which is highest among large banks
Asset quality is robust & credit costs are low.
Bank is investing in collections platform to help expand into self-employed lending segments; can aid growth in FY28-29
Raise core earnings estimated by 2-4%

Nomura on SBI
Neutral, TP Rs 1160
1QFY27 – NIMs surprise positively
Strong PPOP, but deposit lag keeps us Neutral
Margin surprises positively; core PPOP beat led by robust NII
Loan growth healthy but deposit growth lags; asset quality resilient

Kotak Inst Eqt on SBI
Buy, TP Rs 1250
Reported 10% yoy earnings growth, led by 10% yoy operating profit growth.
RoE of 15% was driven by solid loan growth (~20% yoy), low credit costs (~25 bps) and NIM recovering to 3% levels.
Asset quality continues to show are still on benign side of credit cycle
Execution by bank is better or at par with frontline banks at this stage of cycle, which would allow it to trade at elevated multiples.

items.title: RT Omid Memarian: 1/ Chilling statistics and a stark warning from one of Iran’s most prominent economists: In a major essay published in Iran’s Dony...
items.description_html:
RT Omid Memarian
1/ Chilling statistics and a stark warning from one of Iran’s most prominent economists: In a major essay published in Iran’s Donya-ye Eqtesad newspaper, economist Masoud Nili argues that Iran has reached a historic crossroads. The data paint a picture of an economy under extraordinary strain and of a country facing a choice between two fundamentally different models of governance.

Here are some of his key findings:

2/ Since early 2018, the exchange rate has increased nearly 50-fold. In comparable periods before, it had risen by no more than fourfold. This happened through seven major currency crises that repeatedly shook Iran’s economy.

Overall prices have increased by more than 19 times, compared with 3.5 to 3.8 times during similar periods in the past. Food prices have risen by more than 34 times.

3/ Since 2018, GDP has barely grown, while real per capita national income has fallen by nearly 12%.

Between 2018 and 2024, around 16 million people fell below the poverty line: an increase with no historical precedent.

4/ Since 2019, Iran’s working-age population has grown by about 5 million people, but net employment has increased by only 400,000. An average of just 57,000 new jobs per year.

Of Iran’s 66.5 million working-age population, around 40 million are outside the labor force, while about 2.5 million are unemployed. Young people aged 20 to 29 make up the largest share of both inactive and unemployed populations.

5/ The number of women of working age has increased by 2.6 million, yet female employment has not grown. Instead, 700,000 women’s jobs have disappeared.

In just one year, from spring 2025 to spring 2026, Iran lost about 630,000 industrial jobs, wiping out employment gains accumulated gradually over the previous eight years.

6/ Nili argues that the years since 2018 have brought not only economic deterioration but an extraordinary concentration of national crises, from the November 2019 protests, the January 2020 tragedies, the COVID-19 pandemic, the 2022 protests, the 12-day war, the January 2026 events, and the second phase of the war, all leaving deep psychological scars on Iranian society.

7/ His conclusion is ultimately about governance, not economics. Iran now faces two fundamentally different paths.

One treats governance as an arena of confrontation and perpetual conflict.

The other sees governance as the responsibility to provide stability, peace, economic well-being, and prosperity while safeguarding the country’s dignity and independence.

These two approaches cannot coexist indefinitely. As Iran passes through one of the most turbulent periods in its modern history, only one will ultimately shape its future.

8/ Masoud Nili is not an ordinary commentator. He is a professor of economics at Sharif University of Technology, holds a Ph.D. in Economics from the University of Manchester, served as a senior economic adviser to President Hassan Rouhani, contributed to Iran’s first and second five-year development plans, and has spent decades researching macroeconomics, political economy, and economic development. At the moment, super hardliners are pushing for a more confrontational path, but his analysis and stats make it clear what Iran’s priority should be. Link to the full article in persian: https://donya-e-eqtesad.com/%D8%A8%D8%AE%D8%B4-%D8%B3%D8%B1%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87-28/4287319-%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86-%D9%81%D8%B1%D8%AF%D8%A7-%D8%AA%D8%B5%D9%85%DB%8C%D9%85-%D8%A7%D9%85%D8%B1%D9%88%D8%B2-%D9%81%D8%A7%DB%8C%D9%84-%D8%B5%D9%88%D8%AA%DB%8C

items.title: It is important to separate price action from business performance. Let us understand this with a simple practical example. - Stock price is 1000 - EP...
items.description_html:
It is important to separate price action from business performance.

Let us understand this with a simple practical example.

- Stock price is 1000
- EPS is 40
- So P/E = 25x

Now EPS grows 25% YoY
New EPS = 50

At the same time, stock price corrects 10%
New stock price = 900

Now what is the new P/E?
900 divided by 50 = 18x

So despite earnings increasing, the multiple compresses from 25x to 18x.

This is how valuations reset during time & price corrections.

Few stocks may not be doing well in terms of price action - but that does not automatically imply weak businesses.

As long as earnings growth & visibility remain intact, there is no reason to exit simply because a stock is not moving.

Exiting only because the share price is not moving reflects impatience rather than process.

It makes sense to switch only if a better opportunity is available or if the original thesis is no longer valid.

Markets move through sector rotations. One sector comes into favour, while another moves out of favour.

If one keeps chasing whichever sector is currently in momentum, the approach gradually shifts from investing to trading. In that case, strict stop loss discipline becomes essential.

Liquidity & sentiment play a very important role.

Re-rating typically begins when liquidity improves & sentiment turns positive. That is when multiples expand again.

If fundamentals are deteriorating, that is a different discussion altogether. But where earnings continue to compound & valuations have cooled off due to time correction, the setup gradually turns favourable.

items.title: RT Kshitij Anand: After nerding out on 1991 reforms, I found out more things today that I was not aware of: - Chandrashekhar was PM when BOP crisis ca...
items.description_html:
RT Kshitij Anand
After nerding out on 1991 reforms, I found out more things today that I was not aware of:

- Chandrashekhar was PM when BOP crisis came into light and his government initiated IMF Loan sanction process which eventually led to us using our gold as collateral for the loan.

-New Economic Reform that Mr Singh brought to us was apparently heavily inspired by Yashvant Singh’s mini reform which he planned to present in early months of 1991 but couldn’t because he was a part of minority government and couldn’t convince allies and opposition.

RT Ananth Rupanagudi
Early 20th Century, Tiruttangal (Thiruthangal), Madras Presidency. Map of India Before Partition - Vintage Matchbox Art. Thiruthangal is still known for its printing, match-works and fireworks industries.

Hindusthan Match Industries (often labelled as Hindusthan Match Industries, Sivakasi/Tiruttangal) was a classic mid-20th-century safety match manufacturer based in the Madras Presidency (now Tamil Nadu), operating out of the Sivakasi-Tiruttangal region—the historical capital and backbone of India's non-mechanized match production.

Following World War I and the Swadeshi movement, local entrepreneurs in Tamil Nadu—particularly around Sivakasi, Kovilpatti, and Sattur—traveled to hubs like Calcutta (where early match production began around 1910) to learn match-making techniques.

Factories like Hindusthan Match Industries emerged during the British era as part of a flourishing localized cottage and semi-automated industry. The dry climate, affordable labour, and access to softwoods made Tamil Nadu the premier location for scaling manual and semi-automatic match production. #matchbox #industry #history

#WATCH | Delhi: On the impact of the US tariff bill on the Indian economy, Chief Rating Officer at CareEdge Ratings, Sachin Gupta, says, “It will have a multi-order impact on the Indian economy. First of all, we have yet to see how the US implements it, because there is a lot of back-and-forth that happens with many of these US regulations. But assuming that there is indeed a 100% tariff levied, we can analyse this impact at two or three levels. One is the most direct impact, which will be on US imports or Indian exports…if there is indeed a 100% tariff, it becomes unviable…if Russian crude oil supply is excluded from the overall global crude market, where total global crude demand is around 100 million barrels a day, with the Strait of Hormuz accounting for 20 million barrels and Russia accounting for about 9 million barrels, of which India and China take roughly 75% and if both India and China decide not to import from Russia at all due to these 100% tariffs, removing up to 30% of global supply will cause a significant impact. While crude prices have recently been relatively benign at around $70 to $85 a barrel, if this scenario becomes a reality, prices could easily go beyond $100 or even $110 to $120 a barrel, causing India's current account deficit to easily more than double from last year's levels strictly on account of crude. Furthermore, at $110 to $120 a barrel, the government would have to pass on those price rises to the fuel pumps, creating a secondary inflationary impact across the broader economy…”

items.title: In the Indian CDMO landscape, what we saw in the first phase was discovery services, followed by tech transfers for late-stage commercial manufacturin...
items.description_html:
In the Indian CDMO landscape, what we saw in the first phase was discovery services, followed by tech transfers for late-stage commercial manufacturing.

What is being seen now is a migration into the middle part i.e FTE collaboration where WuXi held all the relationships, and this is starting to shift here to India.

Why this matters:

1) Discovery chemistry :- early-stage medicinal chemistry, custom synthesis support. Low ticket size per molecule, but this is where you capture a molecule first.

2) FTE development/collaboration (the middle) :- dedicated scientist teams billed on a time-and-materials basis, doing process development, route scouting, and scale-up as a molecule moves through Phase I/II/III. This is iterative, relationship-heavy work, not a fixed-fee deliverable.

3) Commercial manufacturing :- large-scale API/intermediate production post-approval.

WuXi's edge was never any single stage; rather, it was owning the relationship through the middle, so molecules they touched in discovery naturally migrated to them for commercial manufacturing later. India's first wave (Divi's, Laurus, etc.) largely won stage 3 via tech-transfer on already-late-stage molecules, skipping the relationship capture. Discovery-stage players (Syngene, Sai Life's own discovery arm, Antherm) won stage 1 in isolation.

The gap has been the FTE middle, and that's what Sai Life is now saying it's building out. Owning it means:

(a) Higher stickiness :- once you're embedded in a client's development work, you follow the molecule to commercial scale rather than losing it to a tech-transfer competitor; and

(b) Better economics :- FTE billing during development typically carries better margins than late-stage generic API work.

But this is very early-stage development, and it remains to be seen how things move from here.

Disclaimer - not a recommendation to buy/sell

The answer perhaps lies in point 12 of the Monetary Policy Statement:
"The outlook, however, is hazy because of the uncertainties regarding south-west monsoon, El Niño, geopolitics and global trade policy. There is a need for greater clarity to emerge, especially regarding inflation, its path and composition before taking any policy action. Any such action would also have to consider the need for recalibration of policy rates in line with the evolving growth-inflation dynamics, especially the normalisation of the underlying inflation from its benign levels seen hitherto."

Factfulness is recognizing when a lonely number seems impressive (small or large), and remembering that you could get the opposite impression if it were compared with or divided by some other relevant number.

To control the size instinct, get things in proportion.

items.title: RT Steven N. Durlauf: The treatment of Sanjay Reddy @sanjaygreddy is disgraceful. He is a key figure in the Economics Department of the New School and...
items.description_html:
RT Steven N. Durlauf
The treatment of Sanjay Reddy @sanjaygreddy is disgraceful. He is a key figure in the Economics Department of the New School and is one of the most trenchant critiques of neoclassical economics anywhere. I profoundly disagree with most of what he has to say, but that is of no importance. What is important is that that he is a key thinker on the limits of mainstream economics. To the extent that this action inhibits his future contributions, the discipline is the poorer.

More broadly developments at The New School are terrible news for the academy. The New School's championship of heterodox thinking and scholarly dissent has played and plays a unique role in the ecology of knowledge creation for economics and for social science.

The treatment of Sanjay Reddy @sanjaygreddy is disgraceful. He is a key figure in the Economics Department and one of the most trenchant critiques of neoclassical economics anywhere. I profoundly disagree with most of what he has to say, but that is the point. To the extent that this action inhibits his future contributions, the discipline is the poorer.

He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that. His reasons may be good, and no one may have been able to refute them. But if he is equally unable to refute the reasons on the opposite side; if he does not so much as know what they are, he has no ground for preferring either opinion...Nor is it enough that he should hear the arguments of adversaries from his own teachers, presented as they state them, and accompanied by what they offer as refutations. That is not the way to do justice to the arguments, or bring them into real contact with his own mind. He must be able to hear them from persons who actually believe them; who defend them in earnest, and do their very utmost for them.

John Stuart Mill, On LibertyCrisis at The New School@TheNewSchool

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/05/nyregion/new-school-faculty-fired-nyc.html

The order book is tilting toward export industrials and PV. A ₹950 crore peak annual revenue pipeline and mostly export-oriented industrial and passenger-vehicle programs is already ramping up and will reshape the revenue mix over the next 2-3 years.

Management is guiding for high-teens volume growth. A new product stream (250 kg to 3-ton parts) starts contributing from Q3/Q4 FY28-29 onwards.

This is how all macros and markets should be reported on. 😀


Lee Roach: My wife left me today. She said it was because I “never stop talking.” I said the yen carry trade is a $20 trillion leveraged bet that the Bank of Japan will never normalize rates and she said “I’m taking the dog.”

items.description_html:
RT Alec Stapp
Cloudflare is a $100 billion American company with 5,500 employees.

Its president and co-founder is an immigrant who was able to build the company in the US because of Optional Practical Training (OPT).

Here's what she has to say about the program:

“The best thing the U.S. government has done on immigration is OPT to allow international students a chance to stay and work for a time after graduation.”

OPT gave her the opportunity to refine “the business plan that helped create the company."

Charging a $100k fee on OPT would nuke a critical pathway for recruiting & retaining global talent.



Jeremy Neufeld: These immigrant founders of billion-dollar companies first came to the US as students.

A $100,000 fee on OPT would have lost us many of them.

Founders like these would be eligible for an O-1 today, after they've built their companies. But not when they were getting started.

It would result in US Treasuries looking more attractive compared to emerging markets. I don't see that as a big threat because there are chances of good inflows coming into the capital market because of the recent announcements. In fact, the data that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor spoke about regarding Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) deposits—we are already looking at some $28–30 billion that has already come through FCNR. And then, as I mentioned, through Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) also, we have seen an improvement. On top of that, even if you look at Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) flows, the net FDI flows, the data that we have for the year so far, we have already got some $6 billion of net FDI flows. As against the whole of last year, when we had around $6 billion of net FDI flows, this year, in the first two months, we have already got more than $6 billion. So even on the FDI front, while gross FDI flows have been recording heavy growth, we expect the net FDI flows to also improve in the current fiscal year…”

Going forward, the RBI is going to see how the growth and inflation data pans out, and based on that, there could be rate action in the subsequent meetings later in the year. items.title: There's a lot of discussion about Energy Security. Not enough about Edible oil security. India imports 60% of all our seed oils, and 90% of Palm oils ...
items.description_html:
There's a lot of discussion about Energy Security. Not enough about Edible oil security. India imports 60% of all our seed oils, and 90% of Palm oils (mainly from Malaysia and Indonesia). The largest agri-economy has yet to secure its kitchen oils.

Both Indonesia and Malaysia are now levying export curbs and increasing domestic palm oil blending mandates for domestic energy production. Indonesia is already transitioning from B30 to mandatory B40 and planned B50 biodiesel blending, reducing global export availability. Malaysia is similarly expanding domestic palm oil blending mandates.

Bottomline: There is a massive shift amongst countries towards reducing crude oil imports and blending is the way forward. Ethanol in India, Crude Palm oil (CPO) for them.

Indonesia’s palm oil curbs could open the door for India to step up. What was earlier just an agri-policy (National Mission on Edible Oils) will soon be National priority. And unlike Energy security which is more challenging, this is an easier to solve problem. The acceleration is visible. Telangana and AP have championed the India Palm Oil mission, many more states are coming up now.

Which company fills the void? That's for investors to figure out. A good opportunity in the making.

Read:
https://www.fortuneindia.com/opinion/indonesias-palm-oil-curbs-could-open-the-door-for-india-to-step-up/150389

items.title: Ten Important Filings that you should know, for week ended 24th July 🌯 All data via https://thewrap.in 1. HFCL to expand Data Centre Connectivity c...
items.description_html:
Ten Important Filings that you should know, for week ended 24th July 🌯

All data via https://thewrap.in

1. HFCL to expand Data Centre Connectivity capacity by nearly 5x

HFCL will invest ₹215 crore to add capacity for 270,000 MMC and SNMT assemblies annually, with commissioning expected by September 2027

The capex represents a significant scale up while also shifting HFCL toward higher value connectivity products used inside AI and hyperscale data centers

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/7677aa47-7778-42cc-8404-83ff35875284.pdf

2. Paras Defence has signed a MoU to set up advanced packaging OSAT facility at cost of 6200cr

Advanced packaging is one of the crucial bottlenecks in AI supply chain today. TSMC overflow is already benefiting companies like ASE Tech and Amkor

Paras wants to set up latest 2.5D/3D advanced packaging line

This is just a MoU at this stage and no funding and terms have been finalized

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/f78828b7-aedc-4412-a05f-33fafd4aaefb.pdf

3. SPEL Semiconductor plans major expansion and fundraising of up to ₹1,000 crore

SPEL has approved raising up to ₹500 crore through a Rights Issue/QIP and another ₹500 crore through overseas instruments including FDI or FCCBs

SPEL currently operates a semiconductor packaging and testing facility, it does not manufacture chips or wafers

It packages fabricated semiconductor dies into finished ICs and performs electrical and reliability testing

The funds will be used to modernize and expand its packaging, testing, automation and manufacturing infrastructure
The company also plans to apply for Central and State semiconductor incentives

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/90be6dd5-03e3-4a54-a9c0-a4ba4a1f8183.pdf

4. ICE Make enters into a joint venture with Japanese company Galilei to foray into HoReCa segment

Galilei will also invest 180cr in ICE Make via preference shares

Food Processing & Hospitality already contributes 15-20% of ICE Make’s revenue, while commercial freezers account for only 2%, leaving significant headroom to build a larger standardized HoReCa equipment business

Galilei brings established Japanese product technology and has around 30% share of Japan’s domestic commercial-refrigerator production

https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/corporate/ICEMAKE_24072026125113_Outcome_of_Board_Meeting_final_2.pdf

5. Apollo Micro Systems receives Indian Navy approval to develop an Autonomous Underwater Surveillance System

Apollo Micro Systems has received a Make-II Prototype Sanction Order to develop SAVIOR-ASW, an unmanned semi-submersible vessel that can operate for extended periods and use acoustic sensors and AI/ML to detect and classify submarines and other underwater threats

The system would represent a first-of-its-kind indigenous capability in India and marks Apollo’s formal entry into autonomous maritime and underwater warfare systems

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/408de015-8d30-40a5-9dc6-87c5bc839242.pdf

6. Marine Electricals wins orders worth 376cr including a major order from Siemens for power distribution system that will be used in a Hyperscaler data center

https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/corporate/MARINE_24072026133342_Signed_Regulation_30_Bagging_of_Order.pdf

7. Gabriel India enters ADAS and automotive electronics through JV with Korea-based HL Klemove

Gabriel India will acquire a 30% stake in HL Klemove India for around ₹935 crore, while the Korean parent will retain the remaining 70% stake

HL Klemove India manufactures ADAS radars, front cameras, autonomous-driving control units and software, along with automotive electronics such as braking and steering ECUs

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/6df251ee-57b5-48ab-836c-60d324de1105.pdf

8. Sona Comstar enters into a partnership with Japanese firm Densco Corporation

Sona Comstar and DENSO will establish two India based joint ventures to develop and manufacture traction motors, inverters, generators and eAxles for electric and hybrid vehicles

The first JV will focus on high voltage liquid cooled powertrain systems for passenger and commercial vehicles, with DENSO holding 51% and Sona Comstar holding 49%. This gives Sona access to DENSO’s inverter and hybrid technology and expands it beyond individual EV components into integrated powertrain systems.

In the second JV, Sona will transfer its existing two-wheeler and three-wheeler electric motor and controller business into a subsidiary. DENSO will acquire a 49% stake at an enterprise valuation of ₹1,750 crore, while Sona retains 51% and management control.

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/79c5700d-fea7-4065-9651-2c9e1365c5db.pdf

9. Indo Tech Transformers enters the 400 kV transformer segment for BESS projects

Indo Tech has received NTPC approval to manufacture 400 kV class transformers for BESS projects, expanding its product portfolio beyond the existing 220 kV range
It has also secured an initial order for two 90 MVA, 400 kV transformers through an EPC contractor

Large grid scale BESS projects require high voltage transformers to connect battery systems to 220 kV and 400 kV transmission networks
NTPC’s recent renewable and BESS tenders include 400/33 kV tie transformers and 400 kV pooling substations

The approval moves Indo Tech into a more technically demanding and higher-value transformer segment and positions it to participate in NTPC’s growing BESS and renewable power evacuation pipeline

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/b7377360-48aa-48ed-a80b-86a90e9b668e.pdf

10. Azad Engineering delivers India’s first indigenous 350 kg thrust class expendable turbojet engine

Azad has manufactured and assembled a 350 kg thrust class turbojet engine designed by DRDO’s Gas Turbine Research Establishment, and delivered the first unit to DRDO

This is not a fighter aircraft engine, it is built for a one time use defence platform, such as a missile or unmanned system, rather than a reusable aircraft

The development is significant because Azad is moving beyond manufacturing individual aerospace components to the complete assembly of an indigenous jet engine, establishing system level manufacturing capabilities in a technology mastered by only a few countries

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/42c23ac8-c9c5-4e79-b588-95de5f941f31.pdf

items.description_html:
🚨 C2C’s auditor has issued a qualified opinion and flagged multiple serious financial and compliance concerns:

1️⃣ Liquidity & Going Concern Risk:
The company is facing a liquidity crisis, with statutory dues unpaid due to lack of funds. Recovery from trade receivables remains uncertain, while operations are heavily dependent on short-term promoter funding. The auditor has raised doubt over C2C’s ability to continue as a going concern. Liquidation Risk

2️⃣ CSR Payments Not Cleared:
CSR expenses were recognised through cheques, creating a book overdraft. However, the cheques were not presented for payment. The auditor noted that the CSR obligation is discharged only when the payment is actually cleared.

3️⃣ Statutory Dues Pending:
Undisputed statutory payments remain unpaid. No provision has been made for possible interest or penalties. Delays in filing statutory returns and weak internal controls were also highlighted.

4️⃣ Labour Code Impact Not Assessed:
The company has not quantified the potential impact of new labour regulations on gratuity, provident fund, wages and other employee benefits.

5️⃣ FEMA Compliance Issues:
Overseas receivables remain unrealised beyond RBI timelines. Applications for regularisation are pending, SOFTEX registration is yet to be approved, and possible penalties have not been provided for.

items.title: We initiated Sansera for our subscribers around 16th December 2025. But the more important thing is how we filtered on this idea. > First key factor w...
items.description_html:
We initiated Sansera for our subscribers around 16th December 2025.

But the more important thing is how we filtered on this idea.

> First key factor we observed was the product mix change, where the company's intent was to gradually move from its ICE component business to Aero/Defence/Semicon (ADS) business.

> This product mix shift was visible from the fact that margins had been improving over the last 2 quarters, and growth was starting to pick up. That's how it came under our filters.

> Going a little deeper, we understood that the kind of things it was doing in the ADS business were quite moated. It had a single-source monopoly on Airbus A350/A320 thrust-reversal gimbals with zero defects over 12 years; hogging (machining from solid billet vs. forging) is a much harder-to-replicate capability for aerospace tolerances.

> Also, in its semiconductor business, it was working with Lam Research, where this year their business is expected to go from $10M to $30M .

> Also, as per our channel checks, they had orders/interest from Rolls-Royce for aero-engine feelers, the MMRFIC JV (navy fuses, radars), and a Tesla ESS order.

> All these things were a confirmation of our thesis that management has the capabilities, and that the product mix is changing for good.

> They have also given strong guidance of ₹8,000 Cr in revenue, with ADS at 20–25% of overall business and blended EBITDA margins moving above the 20% mark.

On top of this, we also visited their facility, where we got to understand the manufacturing complexity involved in the components they make for their ADS business, and their capabilities in precision engineering.

The framework was simple: through scanning, found a business where earnings were breaking out and margins were improving > went through their earnings calls and found the story of the product mix change > mapped out the value chain and tried to understand Sansera's moat in the new business they were focusing on > visited their facility to verify our thesis on the company.

Disclaimer: This is not a recommendation to buy or sell. We continue to hold it in our recommendation portfolio and may change our view at any point in time.

items.title: An elevator pitch on how the industrial gases industry works! You separate air into gases, or you buy rare gases and repackage them. You sell either f...
items.description_html:
An elevator pitch on how the industrial gases industry works!

You separate air into gases, or you buy rare gases and repackage them. You sell either from a plant you own (merchant) or from a plant you build inside a customer's factory (on-site).

On-site is a 15-20 year annuity at thin margins. A merchant is a spot market where the same molecule earns very different money depending on the gas, the distance, and who else is selling nearby.

The whole game is capital, location, and the ability to squeeze extra high-margin gas (argon, liquid) out of a plant you've already built.

But let’s get into interesting details about that -

What does the industry actually sell?

Strip away the chemistry and this is an air-separation business. A cryogenic plant is an Air Separation Unit, or ASU that chills atmospheric air until its components liquefy at their different boiling points, and pipes off oxygen, nitrogen and argon at high purity. Everyone in the industry runs broadly the same technology, so purity differences are marginal (roughly plus-or-minus 5%). The molecule is a commodity. Almost everything interesting happens around the molecule in how it's contracted, delivered, and priced.

The demand base has historically been the heavy stuff: steel and metals, autos, pharma, healthcare, and a thin slice of chemicals and F&B. What's changing the growth story is the sunrise demand from solar and semiconductors, which pull large volumes of nitrogen and, in semis, demand purity that cheaper suppliers struggle to hit. That single shift is why every player in the country is pouring capital into new capacity at the same time.

The top four global MNCs Linde, INOX Air Products, Air Water India and Air Liquide India control roughly 80% of the market.

Below them sit regional, owner-driven players (Ellenbarrie, Vayu, Shree Ram Oxygas and similar) who have been around 10–15 years and whose space widened after COVID, when oxygen subsidies pulled local capital in.

Now let’s understand the 2 engines in this industry separately > on-site vs merchant

Everything downstream flows from one fork in the road: do you build the plant inside the customer's factory, or near a cluster of customers and truck the gas out? These are two genuinely different businesses with different economics, different customers, and different personalities.

> On-site - An anchor customer, usually a large steel plant, issues an RFQ saying, in effect, we need ~1,100–1,800 tonnes of gas a day flowing into our furnace. A supplier builds and operates an ASU on their premises under a Build-Own-Operate (BOO) contract running 15–20 years. The revenue is fixed and stable, so it's underwritten on a modest return — players will accept an operating margin of roughly 10–12%, sometimes pricing the whole thing to a ~10–15% IRR. It is deliberately boring money.

Why fight so hard for boring money? Because it's stable, long-dated and defensive with a 15–20 year foothold that also keeps a rival out of that customer. Contracts signed before roughly 2016–18 carried fatter margins and some still run (a few end around 2035), but the new-build market is now openly competitive on price.

> Merchant business - Here you own the plant, liquefy the output, and sell it as liquid, bulk or cylinders to whoever's within reach. Margins are structurally better but volatile: liquid/bulk runs a ~20–25% bottom line, while cylinder and specialty can reach ~40%. The catch is geography. Oxygen and nitrogen are cheap and heavy, so you can't economically truck them much beyond ~200–300 km before distribution cost (typically 10–12% of revenue) eats you alive. You plant an ASU, draw a 200–300 km radius, and fight for that circle.

The reason branded MNCs earn ~40–45% at the top while a strong regional player earns ~35% isn't a secret formula rather it's scale and mix. A Linde or INOX moves 4,000–5,000 TPD daily; a regional player moves 250–300 TPD. At a small scale, tender-driven medical demand keeps margins decent. But to scale from 300 TPD to 3,000–4,000 TPD you must chase the lower-margin sectors that make up the bulk of the market and that's exactly where pricing and margin pressure begin.

The value chain, end to end

Follow a molecule of oxygen from the atmosphere to the customer and you can see where value is captured and where it leaks.

Stage 1 - Build the plant (the capital gate)
This is a capital-intensive, power-intensive industry, and the entry cost is the first moat. A modest 200–250 TPD on-site plant needs at least INR 300–400 crore of initial capex. Core components are compressors, cold boxes that have to be imported; India makes none of them. Only fabrication and storage tanks (INOX, Cryolor, VRV) are domestic. Build time runs 16–24 months per ASU

Stage 2 - Choose your engineering partner (the quiet moat)
Who actually builds the plant is becoming the real differentiator. The MNCs carry in-house EPC muscle - Linde has Linde Engineering, INOX leans on Air Products' US technology which lets them build large, reliable ASUs and win the technically demanding jobs.
Regional players without that engineering wing increasingly tie up with Chinese OEMs on a sale-of-equipment basis: the Chinese firm builds and exits, and the local player does the O&M. It's cheaper (a 200 TPD plant runs ~INR 100–120 crore via a Chinese vendor vs ~INR 150–200 crore via an MNC), but blue-chip steelmakers (Tata, JSW, SAIL, AM/NS) often won't allow a Chinese machine where they're underwriting 15–20 years of reliability, power efficiency and capital backup, and they pay up for it.

The cost-vs-capability gap
> MNC plant, 200 TPD: ~INR 150–200 crore — technology, reliability, blue-chip acceptance.
> Chinese plant, 200 TPD: ~INR 100–120 crore — cost-optimised, favoured by smaller / secondary steel and rolling mills.
> No Indian regulation restricts Chinese ASUs, so the split is driven purely by which customer is buying.

Stage 3 - Extract the by-products (where margin hides)
A basic ASU makes oxygen and nitrogen. To pull argon you must bolt on a separate argon-recovery column and here's the quirk: that column costs roughly the same whether the plant is small or large, but a small 200 TPD ASU yields only ~5–6 TPD of argon while a big ASU yields 50–60 TPD. The capital-to-recovery maths favours scale heavily, yet argon's economics are so attractive that even smaller players are now installing the column anyway.

Stage 4 - Distribute (the tyranny of distance)
Oxygen and nitrogen are regional products which are heavy, cheap, and uneconomic beyond ~300 km. Argon is a national product valuable enough to ship across the country, though distribution then runs ~17–18% of revenue rather than 10–12%. This distinction quietly shapes the entire competitive map: oxygen/nitrogen competition is local and radius-bound, while argon competition is national and cyclical.

How to judge any player in this industry?
Pulling the mechanics together, a handful of questions separate a structurally strong operator from a fragile one regardless of the name on the door.

> Capacity trajectory: Can they actually double liquid capacity? You can't sell a molecule if you can't make expansion of 200 TPD takes 1.5 - 2 years, not six months.

> Mix quality: How much on-site annuity vs volatile merchant? How much argon and by-product upside are they extracting per plant?

> Engineering independence: In-house EPC, or dependent on Chinese OEMs who build and exit? This gates which customers they can win.

> Geographic competition: Are their plants in pockets with few rivals inside the 300 km radius, or in contested western/central India?

> Blue-chip acceptance: Can they clear the reliability/purity bar for Tata, JSW, AM/NS, and semiconductors or are they confined to secondary, cost-driven demand?

> Cycle timing: Are they adding capacity into the current glut, and can their balance sheet and geography absorb 2–3 years of merchant price erosion before demand catches up?

Dislaimer - not a recommendation to buy/sell

Creative Newtech has done an interesting acquisition, transforming from a distributor to a manufacturer of an integrated surveillance technology platform.

Creative Newtech has approved the acquisition of 100% of Infinova (India) for up to US$4 million, marking a strategic shift beyond distribution into surveillance technology manufacturing.

The acquisition brings Infinova's India operations, brand rights, technical expertise, experienced workforce, and local assembly & manufacturing facility, providing Creative Newtech with immediate execution capabilities.

More importantly, the deal lays the foundation for a 'Make in India' surveillance platform, enabling the company to build proprietary products, strengthen after-sales support, and reduce dependence on third-party distribution.

The transaction also accelerates Creative's transition from a distribution-led business to an integrated, technology-led surveillance solutions provider, giving it greater control over manufacturing, product ownership, and margins.

The company holds all the relevant licenses from Gem, BIS, and STQC, enabling it to access the government portal. STQC shifts 22% market share from Chinese to Indian brands

This is more than an acquisition—it is a business model transformation, positioning Creative Newtech to move up the value chain from distributing surveillance products to designing, assembling, and manufacturing them under a 'Make in India' strategy.

Creative NewTech trades at 18 PE vs Prizor Vtech 42PE vs Aditya Infotech 110PE

Great Punjabi Lala Jagat Narain.
He spent years in prison for opposing both British rule and the Emergency. He built Punjab Kesari into one of Punjab's most widely read newspapers and refused to bow before terror.

He stood up to Bhindranwale despite repeated threats. He was assassinated for his courage. The sacrifices did not end there-his son, Ramesh Chander, was also killed, along with 52 members of the Punjab Kesari family.

The media group lost:
• 2 Editors
• 7 Reporters
• 20 Distribution Agents
• 23 Hawkers
• 2 Workers

Their only "crime" was refusing to surrender to Khalistani intimidation and continuing to print the truth.

Punjab Kesari also raised funds and supported the families of Hindu and Sikh civilians murdered by Khalistani terrorists when the state had largely failed them.

When fear forced distributors to stop carrying the newspaper, KPS Gill ensured copies were distributed through police stations so the voice of truth would not be silenced.

Lala Jagat Narain, the Punjab Kesari family, and KPS Gill remind us that Punjab was saved not only by brave security personnel but also by fearless journalists and ordinary citizens who refused to bow before terror.

Their sacrifice must never be forgotten. 🇮🇳

items.title: RT Sagar Awatade: I don't know who else to tell this to, so I am going to tell my story here. Every day is a struggle for a young business, but the la...
items.description_html:
RT Sagar Awatade
I don't know who else to tell this to, so I am going to tell my story here.

Every day is a struggle for a young business, but the last few months have been harder than usual.

We are a small Indian company. For more than ten years we have been building a homegrown brand in a product category dominated by big foreign players.

There are almost no Indian names in this space. We set out to be one.

We started in 2014. Over the years we began making parts in India instead of just importing, and we started selling in the US, Dubai, Nepal, Malaysia and South Africa.

We showed up at global trade fairs to represent an Indian brand on the world stage.

In 2023 we changed the import code we use for our product. We did not do this quietly. Every shipment was declared. Nothing was hidden. We didn't invent our approach.

We followed written professional advice and the way this product is treated in markets around the world.

And now we are facing a government demand running into tens of crores in duty recovery and penalties, plus personal penalties on the founders and even on an employee.

For a company our size, this is not a fine we can pay and move on from. This ends us.

We have not run from any of this. I am not built like that. It is not how I was raised. We have written to the authorities, met officials in person, and we have now filed a writ in the High Court.

All we are asking for is a fair treatment.

I set out to build in India and sell to the world. I am asking only that the system back honest founders trying to compete globally, instead of breaking them.

The process is the process, and it exists for a reason. But process should not feel like punishment.

From where I am standing today, it does.
I am not giving up. I have worked too hard for this. If you have read this far, please share it. If you know someone who can help, point them my way. Help me get the word out.

Exactly 10 years ago in May 2016, i went to a session on bootstrapping at TiE event in Santa Clara. That changed my life.

When i spent time in bay area working on advanced sensing technologies in semicon space, everything was there in life(money, granted patents, travelling to new country every month, wife, so called good life) but it still felt empty within.

Was burning a lot of midnight oil trying to build something, failed twice trying to build in US. Those failures hit hard and made me realise that everthing that i had was only beacuse of the company that i was working for, i was zero outside of it.

During this phase is when i first met @svembu ji, did not know who he was, did not know about zoho. He was wearing a plain simple green kurtha, jeans and slippers gving a session on bootstraping his company. I asked "can we bootstrap a hardware business too ?" And he said " why not ? "

This along with zoho story, made my conviction of moving back to India stronger, it took almost a week for me to digest what zoho was and what was built without raising a single dime from VCs and i felt so proud and blessed to have met the man behind.

Moved back to India same year in October. It was only about building something here which makes sense in long term, something which was ignored by people for a long time.

Ofcourse it came at a cost, divorce, hard time telling people not to worry about me or my personal life, making sure that my parents are not suffering, isolating all the peronal stuff with the vision of building strong electronics manufacutring ecosystem in India.

10 years FF- we are a strong team of 200+, bootstrapped, growing fast, building factories in India which can compete globally soon. On a personal level, i still hardly spend few thousand rupess everymonth, lead a minimal life, have a loving wife who belives in me and a kid who is growing fast, parents who are proud that i am doing something in India.

There is no multimillion dollars in my bank as safety, my kid and wife are Indians with Indian passport and my parents were teachers/avg govt employee without any background in business.

I dont feel empty inside me, anymore. Fire inside me is for building India's electronics manufacturing capacity that can compete globally, a strong ecosystem for next gen to build products from India and a strong team that can run this beyond me.

Jai Hind!🇮🇳

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.description_html: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely rare to see the Mid & Small cap indices (avg of the two) beating the Nifty 50 near the bottom of the cycle. Their avg CAGR has outperformed during the last two tough years as well as all the below trailing years. I am not that surprised as their balance sheet, P&L and cash flow quality has substantially improved post COVID. I believe the biggest multi-baggers will emerge from this space as the earnings growth differential will be significant going forward. Because of the quality differential today vs during pre-COVID period, I would be surprised if their valuations correct to levels seen during the previous crashes. We probably have the best corporate quality and least stressed financials currently compared to any other previous big crisis.

items.title: RT Anil Agarwal: It is painful to see India face the adverse consequences of a war we have nothing to do with, particularly because of raw material se...
items.description_html:
RT Anil Agarwal
It is painful to see India face the adverse consequences of a war we have nothing to do with, particularly because of raw material security. We don’t have to import 90% of our oil, or 95% of our copper or 99.5% of our gold or any other metal resources. Mother Earth has given us the best geology. Last 40 years of practice in the minerals, metals and oil industry have taught me this. Now is the time, with this positive government, to give entrepreneurs freedom.

At just 19, I came to Bombay from Bihar and built a company in this industry from scratch. Vedanta was able to acquire Hindustan Zinc and BALCO under a privatisation programme which was never completed. 26% and 49% stakes are still held by the government and not been transferred as per a predetermined agreement. Vedanta also acquired ONGC Oil and Gas asset via UK’s Cairn and Sesa Goa Iron ore from Japan’s Mitsui.

In each one, the ambition and goal was to increase the production so much that India wouldn’t need to import but, in fact export. In Hindustan Zinc and BALCO, we succeeded. We increased zinc production 10 times, 20 times in aluminium. In the process, more than 1,000 companies have come up for processing this raw material. And Vedanta has contributed Rs 4.5 lakh crore to the exchequer in the last ten years. In oil and gas, our vision is to produce 1 million barrels per day. In iron ore, my vision is to produce 100 million tonnes, 33% of today’s production level. There are many more underperforming government assets that can perform the same way.

Three or four decades ago, there was no know-how, no experts, no finance in this industry. It took a lot of determination. Vedanta raised 35 billion USD from abroad and invested in India. It brought experts and technology. Because of that, Hindustan Zinc can also produce silver and fertiliser, and we are working very hard to start producing critical minerals very soon, something we were told would never happen in India.

Globally, only few very large companies engage in mining as it is very difficult without scale. Vedanta should be for India what Rio Tinto and BHP are for Australia or Vale is for Brazil. Other entrepreneurs and companies must create new Vedantas.

Most of the advanced countries have become prosperous by developing natural resources, including oil and gas. In India, the system has to stop creating hurdles. It needs to take a long-term view, as this government is not revenue-minded but, production-minded. It must facilitate. Instead of notices and judicial activity, all businesses need to receive recognition and respect. Benefit of doubt should pass onto them.

In India, we have economic heroes who can raise production equal to the biggest and best in the world. We should not allow tunnel vision or outdated mindset to keep us small and dependent. Some may remember the case of Rio Tinto which had invested in a diamond mine in Madhya Pradesh. It could have made India a global hub for diamond production, but they exited because of a complex, interfering and discouraging system.

The most important thing is trust. Keep the system simple, keep regulation limited and you eliminate the root cause of wrongdoing. We should have self-certification instead of lengthy approvals and clearances. The Government issues the rulebook and entrepreneurs strictly comply, subject to audit. Constant enquiry and interference only discourage enterprise. Also, the mindset of discrimination between public sector and private sector should change.

This year my family had the biggest tragedy. It was heartening to hear the words of the Prime Minister who said, “You must stay strong and continue to do work which is important for India.” That is the motivation of my life. I have the blessings of my grandfather and grandmother, who spent 40 years in Vrindavan in a small hut, in Manav Seva Sangh with their guruji, Swami Sharnanand Ji Maharaj. They always advised me, if you have wealth, you must use it for society. If you don’t have wealth, you must always help society with your hand. We all are willing to work hard, take risks and ensure that India becomes self-sufficient. The system should encourage us to deliver for our society and nation; this will eradicate unemployment and encourage women empowerment. This sector has given the maximum revenue to the exchequer in India and in the world for nation-building. It will help in making our country a developed nation, as envisioned by our Prime Minister. Let’s make India & Indians proud.

items.title: As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/Mar...
items.description_html:
As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/March trough—are not an exception; they are a recurring feature of market cycles. Just as consistently, these phases have been followed by sharp recoveries once the market establishes a bottom in February or March.
Current sentiment is such that investors are overly focused on the negatives, making the environment appear so foggy that positives have become invisible. This fog, as always, will eventually lift.

While market bottoms and the depth of drawdowns can never be predicted, it is highly probable that market levels a few months from now will be disproportionately higher. Unfortunately, short-term declines are unsettling for investors, causing many to step aside and miss the eventual strong upswing.

In hindsight, this phase will look like an obvious opportunity. But while living through it, investors see only risks and landmines—never the runway for the next flight
